quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the three primary motions, the parts of a loom and the vocabulary of a construction.

questions.q: Which loom motion divides the warp into two sheets so that the weft can pass between them?
questions.explain: Shedding raises some ends and lowers others to open a shed. Picking is the motion that then carries the weft through that shed, not the one that opens it.

questions.q: Which part of the loom pushes the newly inserted pick against the fell of the cloth?
questions.explain: Beating-up is done by the reed, which swings forward and packs the pick against the fell. The healds only lift and lower ends; they never touch the weft.

questions.q: Picking is the motion that carries the weft across the loom through the open shed.
questions.explain: Yes: picking inserts the weft by shuttle, projectile, rapier or a jet of air or water. Shedding opens the path and beating-up fixes the pick afterwards.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three primary motions of a loom?
questions.explain: Let-off (feeding warp from the beam) and take-up (winding the cloth) are secondary motions that keep the process continuous; the three primary motions are shedding, picking and beating-up.

questions.q: The fell of the cloth is best described as:
options: The line where the last pick has just been beaten up
The selvedge at each side of the fabric
The point where the warp leaves the beam
The roller on which woven cloth is wound
questions.explain: The fell is the edge of the woven cloth where each new pick is beaten in. A starting mark appears when the loom is restarted without putting the fell back in its correct position.

questions.q: What does the take-up motion do?
options: Winds the woven cloth away from the fell
Selects which ends rise on each pick
Cuts the weft at the selvedge
questions.explain: Take-up winds the cloth forward at a steady rate; let-off is its partner that feeds warp from the beam. Selecting ends is shedding.

questions.q: The weft can be inserted by a shuttle, a projectile, a rapier, or a jet of air or water.
questions.explain: All five are picking methods named in the lecture. Shuttle looms carry a pirn of weft; the others take weft from a stationary supply package.

questions.q: In the construction 20 × 16 / 128 × 60, 63", 3/1, what does the figure 16 stand for?
questions.explain: The first pair is warp count × weft count, so 16 is the weft count in Ne. The second pair, 128 × 60, is ends × picks per inch; 63" is the width and 3/1 the weave.

questions.q: In the English (Ne) system the yarn count is the number of:
questions.explain: Ne counts hanks (leas) of 840 yards per pound, so a finer yarn has a higher number. Grams per 1,000 m is the tex system, a direct count where a higher number means coarser yarn.

questions.q: Which pair of figures in a construction tells you how closely the cloth is set?
questions.explain: Ends per inch and picks per inch describe the sett, the thread density. The counts describe how fine the yarns are, and width and weave are separate items.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How total ends, loom picks, warp yarn length and the quick GSM rule are built, and which way each moves when an input changes.

questions.q: The total number of ends in a warp is found from:
options: Ends per inch × width in inches
Picks per inch × width in inches
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width, e.g. 128 × 63 = 8,064 in the lecture. Picks per inch relate to the weft, not the warp, and the count has nothing to do with how many ends there are.

questions.q: A finished cloth must have 60 picks per inch and contracts 8 % in length after leaving the loom. Which expression gives the picks per inch to set on the loom?
questions.explain: The cloth shrinks, so the same picks crowd into less length; the loom must insert fewer: 60 × 0.92 = 55.2. Multiplying by 1.08 or dividing by 0.92 would put MORE picks on the loom, the wrong direction.

questions.q: More picks per inch are inserted on the loom than are counted in the finished cloth.
questions.explain: The reverse is true. Because the fabric contracts in length after the loom, fewer picks are inserted per inch on the loom (55.2 in the lecture) than are counted in the finished cloth (60).

questions.q: In the quick rule GSM ≈ (EPI/Ne warp + PPI/Ne weft) × 25, what happens to the estimate if the warp count changes from 20s to 30s with the same ends per inch?
questions.explain: Ne is an indirect count: 30s is finer than 20s, so the warp term EPI/Ne gets smaller and the fabric is lighter. Students often read a bigger count number as a heavier yarn; in Ne it is the opposite.

questions.q: Why are the yards of warp yarn per yard of fabric (8,870) more than the total ends (8,064)?
options: Because of crimp: each end bends over and under the picks
Because the reed stretches the ends
questions.explain: Each end is longer than the cloth it lies in because it waves over and under the weft; the worksheet allows about 10 % crimp, 8,064 × 1.10 ≈ 8,870. Weft is a separate calculation.

questions.q: Use the quick rule GSM ≈ (EPI/Ne warp + PPI/Ne weft) × 25 for the lecture's drill 20 × 16 / 128 × 60. Give the GSM to one decimal place.
questions.explain: Warp term 128 ÷ 20 = 6.40; weft term 60 ÷ 16 = 3.75; sum 10.15 × 25 = 253.75 g/m², which the worksheet rounds to 254.

questions.q: If the ends per inch are doubled while everything else stays the same, the quick GSM estimate:
options: Rises by the warp term only
Is unchanged because GSM is per square metre
questions.explain: Only the warp term EPI/Ne doubles; the weft term PPI/Ne is unchanged, so the total rises by less than double. GSM is per square metre, but doubling the ends in every inch does change the weight of that square metre.

questions.q: Which statement about the Ne count is correct?
options: A 40s yarn is coarser than a 20s yarn
A 40s yarn has 40 × 840 yards in one pound
A 40s yarn weighs 40 grams per 1,000 metres
A 40s yarn has 40 yards in one hank
questions.explain: 40s means 40 hanks of 840 yd per pound, i.e. 33,600 yd/lb, so it is finer than 20s. Grams per 1,000 m is tex, and a hank is always 840 yd.

questions.q: In the indirect (Ne) count system a higher number means a coarser yarn.
questions.explain: In an indirect system the number is length per fixed weight, so more hanks per pound means a thinner yarn. Higher number = finer in Ne; higher number = coarser only in direct systems such as tex or denier.

questions.q: Length contraction after the loom affects which of the worksheet's results?
options: Picks per inch to set on the loom
questions.explain: Contraction shortens the cloth, so only the loom picks per inch are adjusted (60 → 55.2). The number of ends is fixed by EPI × width and the yarn counts are properties of the yarn.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Construction arithmetic: total ends, loom picks, warp yarn length and quick GSM for the lecture's fabric and some new ones.

questions.q: A fabric has 128 ends per inch and is 63 inches wide. How many ends are in the warp?
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width = 128 × 63 = 8,064 ends, the figure in the lecture worksheet.

questions.q: A finished cloth is to have 60 picks per inch and the fabric contracts 8 % in length after leaving the loom. What picks per inch should be set on the loom? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Loom PPI = finished PPI × (1 − contraction) = 60 × 0.92 = 55.2 picks per inch; the lecture rounds this to 55.

questions.q: A warp of 8,064 ends is woven with 10 % crimp. How many yards of warp yarn go into each yard of fabric? Round to the nearest yard.
questions.explain: Each end supplies 1.10 yd per yard of cloth because of crimp, so 8,064 × 1.10 = 8,870.4 ≈ 8,870 yd, matching the worksheet.

questions.q: Estimate the GSM of a sheeting 30 × 30 / 76 × 68 using GSM ≈ (EPI/Ne warp + PPI/Ne weft) × 25.
A fabric is set at 72 ends per inch and woven 58 inches wide. How many ends must be on the weaver's beam?
questions.explain: 72 × 58 = 4,176 ends. The weft count and picks play no part in the number of ends.

questions.q: A finished fabric needs 72 picks per inch and the length contraction after the loom is 10 %. What picks per inch are set on the loom? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: 72 × 0.90 = 64.8 picks per inch on the loom; after 10 % contraction these become 64.8 ÷ 0.9 = 72 in the cloth.

questions.q: Estimate the GSM of a poplin 40 × 40 / 133 × 72 with the quick rule GSM ≈ (EPI/Ne + PPI/Ne) × 25. Round to the nearest whole number.
A warp has 4,176 ends and the crimp is 10 %. How many yards of warp yarn are used per yard of fabric?
questions.explain: 4,176 × 1.10 = 4,593.6 ≈ 4,594 yd. 3,758 would be 4,176 × 0.90, subtracting crimp instead of adding it; 4,176 ignores crimp altogether.

questions.q: How many yards of yarn are there in one pound of 20s Ne yarn? (One hank = 840 yd.)
questions.explain: 20s means 20 hanks per pound and each hank is 840 yd, so 20 × 840 = 16,800 yd per pound.

questions.q: A finished fabric has 60 picks per inch and is 63 inches wide. Ignoring crimp, how many yards of weft are in one yard (36 in) of fabric?
questions.explain: Picks per yard = 60 × 36 = 2,160; each pick is 63 in = 1.75 yd long; 2,160 × 1.75 = 3,780 yd of weft per yard of cloth.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Reading faults on the inspection table and sorting out construction problems in the weaving office.

questions.q: An inspector finds a thin line running straight across the width of the cloth. What is the most likely defect?
questions.explain: A pick runs across the cloth, so a missing pick leaves a thin line across the width; a missing end leaves a thin line along the length. The usual cause is a weft break that was not detected.

questions.q: A band of lower pick density appears across the fabric. The weaver confirms the loom was stopped for a warp break and restarted. What is the defect and its cause?
options: Double pick — two picks in one shed
Reed mark — too many ends per dent
Crack (starting mark) — fell not corrected before restarting
questions.explain: A crack or starting mark is a band of thin pick density caused by restarting the loom without putting the fell back in the right place. A double pick gives a thick bar, the opposite symptom.

questions.q: A cloth shows faint streaks running along the warp direction at regular spacing. What should the weaving manager check first?
options: The number of ends per dent in the reed
questions.explain: Warp-way streaks are reed marks, caused by too many ends per dent for the yarn; a reed with more dents per inch (fewer ends per dent) is the cure. The weft package and shuttle affect picks, not warp-way marks.

questions.q: A thick weft bar appears across the cloth. Which defect is this and what usually causes it?
options: Double pick — two picks inserted in one shed
questions.explain: Two picks in one shed make a double pick, seen as a thick bar. A missing pick would look thin, not thick.

questions.q: Floats on the cloth are usually caused by ends sticking together or a late shed.
questions.explain: If ends cling together or the shed opens late, some ends are not where they should be when the weft passes, so the thread skips over several others and a float appears.

questions.q: A thin line runs along the length of the fabric for several metres. Which protective device has most likely failed?
questions.explain: A line along the length means a missing end, caused by a warp break the warp stop motion did not catch. The weft stop motion guards against missing picks (lines across).

questions.q: A pick is seen to stop part-way across the width of the fabric. What is this called and why does it happen?
options: Half pick — the pick broke during insertion
questions.explain: A half pick is a pick that stops part-way across because the weft broke during insertion. A float is a thread skipping over others, not a pick ending early.

questions.q: A weaver sets 60 picks per inch on the loom for a cloth specified at 60 picks per inch finished, forgetting the 8 % length contraction. What happens?
options: The finished cloth has about 55 picks per inch and is too light
The finished cloth has about 65 picks per inch, is heavier and uses more weft than costed
questions.explain: After 8 % contraction the 60 loom picks crowd into 0.92 in, giving 60 ÷ 0.92 ≈ 65 picks per inch: heavier cloth and more weft consumption than quoted. The correct loom setting was 55.2.

questions.q: A customer orders 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 at 63" width, but a beam already dressed in the store has 7,680 ends. At 128 ends per inch, what width will that beam weave?
questions.explain: Width = total ends ÷ EPI = 7,680 ÷ 128 = 60 in, three inches short of the order. The beam cannot be used as it is; a 63" cloth needs 8,064 ends.

questions.q: Which defect is the most direct evidence that an end broke and the loom carried on weaving?
questions.explain: A missing end means a warp break was not detected by the stop motion, so the loom kept weaving without that end. The other three are weft or restart faults.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that chain two steps together and catch the common slips in construction arithmetic.

questions.q: Which single change would raise the quick GSM estimate of 20 × 16 / 128 × 60?
questions.explain: A 12s weft is coarser than 16s, so PPI/Ne rises from 3.75 to 5.0 and the cloth gets heavier. Finer warp (24s) or fewer picks lower the weight, and width does not enter a per-square-metre figure.

questions.q: A loom runs at 500 picks per minute and is set to 55.2 picks per inch on the loom. How many inches of cloth does it weave per minute? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Length woven per minute = picks per minute ÷ picks per inch on the loom = 500 ÷ 55.2 = 9.06 in/min. Using the finished 60 PPI here would understate the loom's output.

questions.q: A student calculates the loom setting for a 60-pick finished cloth with 8 % contraction as 60 × 1.08 = 64.8. What is the mistake?
options: Contraction only applies to the warp count
questions.explain: The cloth shortens after weaving, so the loom inserts fewer picks per inch than the finished cloth shows: 60 × (1 − 0.08) = 55.2. Multiplying by 1.08 goes the wrong way and would give an over-heavy cloth.

questions.q: A loom was set at 55.2 picks per inch and the finished cloth measures 60 picks per inch. What was the length contraction, in per cent?
questions.explain: Contraction = 1 − loom PPI ÷ finished PPI = 1 − 55.2 ÷ 60 = 0.08, i.e. 8 %.

questions.q: In the construction 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 the cloth has more ends per inch than picks per inch.
questions.explain: 128 ends per inch against 60 picks per inch: the warp is set more than twice as densely as the weft, which is typical of a warp-faced 3/1 drill.

questions.q: A fabric uses 8,870 yd of 20s Ne warp yarn per yard of cloth. What is the weight of warp per yard of cloth in pounds, to three decimal places? (1 hank = 840 yd.)
questions.explain: 20s yarn has 20 × 840 = 16,800 yd per lb, so 8,870 ÷ 16,800 = 0.528 lb of warp per yard of fabric.

questions.q: A cloth shows a thin line across the width followed immediately by a band of low pick density. What most likely happened?
options: A weft break stopped the loom and it was restarted without correcting the fell
Ends stuck together in the shed
questions.explain: The thin line is a missing pick from a weft break; the band after it is a starting mark because the fell was not reset before restarting. Reed marks run warp-way, and stuck ends give floats.

questions.q: Compare sheeting 30 × 30 / 76 × 68 (about 120 g/m²) with drill 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 (about 254 g/m²). Which statement is correct?
options: The drill is roughly twice the weight because it uses coarser yarns set more closely
The sheeting is heavier because it has more picks
They weigh the same because both are cotton
The drill is lighter because its width is 63 inches
questions.explain: The drill combines coarser yarns (20s, 16s) with a denser warp (128 EPI), so both terms of the quick rule are larger; 254 is just over twice 120. More picks alone do not make the sheeting heavier when its yarns are much finer.

questions.q: Why can a weaver not simply count 60 picks per inch at the fell and expect 60 picks per inch in the finished cloth?
options: Because the reed removes some picks
Because the cloth contracts in length after leaving the loom, packing the picks closer
Because the weft count changes after finishing
Because picks per inch are measured only in the warp direction
questions.explain: Length contraction after the loom pulls the picks closer together, so the finished count is higher than the loom count. The reed does not remove picks and the weft count is fixed.

questions.q: A cloth of 8,064 ends is woven at 55.2 picks per inch on the loom from a weft that is 63 inches wide. How many picks are inserted in 100 yards of loom-state cloth?
questions.explain: 100 yd = 3,600 in; 3,600 × 55.2 = 198,720 picks. The number of ends and the width do not affect how many picks there are in a given length.
